definition.text: The link between spending time in natural surroundings and a person's mental health.

facts.text: Studies count almost any contact with nature as exposure, from a hike or a forest visit to a walk in a park or time by a lake.
Contact with nature is tied to lower stress, better mood, more happiness and meaning, and less mental distress.
An eighteen-year Danish study found children raised with the most green space had 55% less risk of developing several psychiatric disorders.
A 10-year UK study found that greener surroundings within 300m of home and nearby green and blue spaces both lowered the risk of anxiety and depression.
Nature exposure improves working memory, attention and cognitive flexibility, while urban settings have been linked to attention deficits.
Even short exposure helps: students who glimpsed a flowering green roof for 40 seconds made fewer errors on a dull task than those shown a concrete roof.
Modern indoor, screen-heavy lifestyles have reduced people's contact with nature.
Therapists use nature in treatments called ecotherapy.

title: City parks and mental health
article: Nature exposure and mental health#City parks and mental health

definition.text: The benefit that parks inside cities bring to the mental health of the people living near them.

facts.text: Residents living 800m to 1.6km from a park had mental health scores 4.5 points lower than residents within 400m of one.
Urban parks help reduce stress and lower the risk of anxiety and depression.
Being cheap and open to all, urban parks can make mental health benefits accessible regardless of income or background.

definition.text: Travel to enjoy an area's natural attractions, including its plants and animals.

facts.text: It overlaps with wildlife and adventure tourism and includes ecotourism, which focuses on environmental education and conservation.
Variants include stargazing, cycling and birdwatching tourism.
National parks have become closely associated with it.
It can harm the environment, but it can also aid conservation by making remaining natural areas more valuable to local people and landowners.

definition.text: Leisure activity done outdoors, usually in natural settings.

facts.text: Activities range from fishing, hunting and walking to hiking, camping, climbing, kayaking and skiing.
People pursue it for exercise, general wellbeing and spiritual renewal, with less stress on competition than organised sport.
It often takes place in thinly populated areas with mountains, lakes, rivers and scenic views.
In 2024 outdoor recreation accounted for $696.7 billion of value added, 2.4 percent of US GDP, according to the US Bureau of Economic Analysis.
University outdoor programs have been shown to help students' wellbeing and stress levels.
Forest managers count outdoor recreation among the objectives forests serve, alongside timber, conservation and hunting.

definition.text: A natural feature or area of land or water that holds special spiritual meaning for a people or community.

facts.text: They include mountains, forests, groves, trees, rivers, lakes, caves, islands and springs, ranging from a single tree to whole mountain ranges.
They exist on every continent except Antarctica; India alone has at least 13,720 reported sacred groves, with an estimated 100,000 to 150,000 in total.
Many have been protected for long periods with little use, and some are notably rich in biodiversity.
Besides sheltering species, they can supply water, medicines and other ecosystem services and support pilgrimage and tourism.
Some have been governed by taboos excluding women or marginalised groups, so they should not be romanticised.
The Convention on Biological Diversity recognised an urgent need to protect them and in 2004 issued the Akwe Kon guidelines for assessing developments that may affect them.
